What NRP Is

2

What is NRP?

  • One national Kubernetes cluster, Nautilus, for research and education
  • Run by SDSC, Nebraska–Lincoln and MGHPCC; funded by NSF
  • Hardware from 70+ institutions, on research and education networks
  • NJEdge hosts NRP nodes too (orange)
  • Today:
  • 534 nodes at 129 sites
  • 1,460 GPUs in 33 models; 35,448 CPUs
  • 15 PB of raw Ceph storage
  • Free for US nonprofit institutions, community colleges included
  • One team runs it from the OS up: no Kubernetes team needed on your campus
https://dash.nrp-nautilus.io

Containers and Kubernetes

  • Container image: an app and everything it needs, built once from a Dockerfile; runs the same anywhere
  • Kubernetes runs containers across many machines: you declare what you want (an image, CPUs, memory, a GPU), the scheduler picks a node that has it, and controllers keep it that way
  • A running container is a pod. Pods, Jobs, Deployments and Services live in a namespace: one per lab, course or service
  • NRP is one Kubernetes cluster: 534 nodes

NAIRR Classroom

What is a Namespace?

  • Your course's space on the cluster: one per course, lab or project
  • You're its admin, and you add your TAs
  • Your course hub, its storage and anything else you run lives in it
  • Members see their own namespaces, not anyone else's
  • 2,334 of them today

14

Sharing GPUs Fairly

  • Reserved nodes: on request, admins taint a contributor's nodes; only pods that tolerate the taint, the owner's, run there
  • Today: 119 nodes reserved for 23 groups
  • Shared nodes: idle GPUs go to opportunistic pods, the lowest priority class, e.g. OSG jobs for IceCube and LIGO
  • 232 opportunistic pods running, 208 of them from OSG
  • When anyone needs that GPU, the opportunistic pod is preempted: it must checkpoint, or just restart
Reserved node · taint nautilus.io/reservation=lab-a
lab-a podGPU in use

A pod without the toleration can't land on the reserved node, even on an idle GPU.

On a shared node, opportunistic pods fill the idle GPUs.

A normal pod arrives: the scheduler preempts an opportunistic pod to make room.

15

Regions and Storage

  • Every node is labeled with its region, zone (143 zones) and site; workloads spread out or stay near their data
  • Rook runs 9 Ceph clusters, one per region or large site: 14.9 PB raw
  • CephFS for shared files, RBD for block, S3 for objects
  • Linstor (DRBD) for fast replicated block storage; CVMFS for software; local NVMe for scratch
  • Pick the storage in the region where you compute

Ways to Run Work

Interactive: JupyterHub

  • Pick a GPU from the start menu; explore, debug, teach
  • Idle servers stop: 1 hour after you close the browser on NRP's hub, 6 hours at most on any hub

Interactive: a pod

  • Start a container with kubectl, then open a shell in it
  • Deleted after 6 hours; at most 2 GPUs

Long-running: a Deployment

  • Keeps a service up (a web app, a database) and restarts it if it crashes
  • Removed after 2 weeks unless admins grant an exception; no GPU if it sits mostly idle

Batch: a Job

  • Runs your script to the end, then gives the GPU back
  • Submit many at once; the rest wait in Pending for a free GPU
$ kubectl apply -f sweep/        # six training jobs
Pendinglr-0.1lr-0.03lr-0.01lr-0.003lr-0.001lr-0.0003GPU 1GPU 2GPU 3GPU 4lr-0.1lr-0.03lr-0.01lr-0.003lr-0.001lr-0.0003time

Six jobs on four GPUs: two wait in Pending and take the first GPUs that free up. When the last one ends, all four GPUs are free again.

1. Pick a GPU

2. Your notebook runs on it

17

A GPU Job

apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata: {name: gpu-train-daniel, namespace: my-lab}     # (1)spec:  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: Never      containers:      - name: train        image: pytorch/pytorch:2.9.0-cuda13.0-cudnn9-runtime  # (2)        command: ["python", "train.py"]        resources:                                       # (3)          requests: {cpu: "2", memory: 6Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1}          limits:   {cpu: "2", memory: 6Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1}      affinity:                                          # (4)        nodeAffinity:          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:            nodeSelectorTerms:            - matchExpressions:              - {key: nvidia.com/gpu.memory, operator: Gt, values: ["20000"]}              - {key: nvidia.com/gpu.compute.major, operator: Gt, values: ["7"]}

(1) Where: your namespace

(2) What: a container image, and the command to run

(3) Resources: 2 CPUs, 6 GB of memory, one GPU

(4) Which GPU: more than 20 GB, Ampere or newer; or name exact models

18

Using GPUs Fairly

Do

  • Give GPUs only to the menu options that need them
  • Let idle servers stop: keep the culling on
  • Request what students will use; keep limits close to requests
  • Keep data in home folders or the shared volume, not inside the image

Don't

  • Leave servers holding GPUs overnight
  • Give every student 4 GPUs “just in case”: use must stay above 40%
  • Put results on the server's own disk: it vanishes with the server
https://nrp.ai/documentation/userdocs/start/policies/

A class hub, step by step

One URL for the whole class. Behind it: your hub, in your namespace, and the cluster's nodes.

1. Students log in

With their campus account, through CILogon. The hub lets in only the people you allow.

2. Each student gets a server

The hub starts a container for each student, with the image, CPUs, memory or GPU of the option they picked.

3. Their files are there

Each server mounts the student's own home folder, plus a shared course folder everyone reads from.

4. Idle servers stop

After an hour with no activity the server shuts down and its GPU goes back to the pool. The home folder stays for next time.

Who Can Log In

  • Campus login through CILogon: you never hand out or reset passwords
  • Your class list: allow your students by name or email, or a whole campus domain
  • Admins: you and your TAs; an admin can open a student's server to help
  • For a workshop or a demo, a shared password works too: today's demo uses one
Sign inat your hub's URL
CILogonpick your campus
On the list?your hub checks
Ina server starts
Not on itturned away

CILogon connects your hub to your institution's own sign-in, the same one students use for email.

23

Setting Up Campus Login

The login part of values.yaml
hub:  config:    JupyterHub:      authenticator_class: cilogon    CILogonOAuthenticator:      client_id: <from CILogon>        # and its client secret      oauth_callback_url: https://jhub-bio210.nrp-nautilus.io/hub/oauth_callback      allowed_idps:        https://idp.campus.edu/idp/shibboleth:     # your campus's entity ID          username_derivation: {username_claim: email}      admin_users: [you@campus.edu, ta@campus.edu]      allowed_users: [student1@campus.edu, student2@campus.edu]
1. Ask CILogon for a clientfor your hub's address; it's issued by hand, so ask early
2. Look up your campusits entity ID, in the CILogon IdP list
3. Name who gets inadmins, and your class list or your whole campus domain
4. helm upgradestudents who drop lose access at the next upgrade

Allow rules add up: allowed_domains admits a whole campus, allowed_users named people; blocked_users wins over both.

26

Files and Course Material

Home folders

One per student, kept between sessions. You set the size; the demo uses 5 GB.

Course material by link

One link pulls your course's git repository into each student's folder (nbgitpuller). This webinar's launch links work the same way.

Shared data

One shared volume in every server: read-only for students, writable for you. Big datasets live once, not 40 times.

https://jhub-bio210.nrp-nautilus.io/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https://github.com/you/bio210&urlpath=lab/tree/bio210/week3.ipynb

A student clicks it and lands in week 3's notebook; their own edits are kept when the repository updates.

28

Sizing a Class

  • Each server asks for the CPUs, memory and GPU of its menu option; the scheduler sets exactly that aside
  • So set options to what a student really uses, not the most you can get
  • GPU options for the units that need them; the rest of the term on CPUs
  • Idle servers stop, so a class only holds resources while it works
  • Tell the NRP team your class size and your lab times

40 students on the Python option: 2 CPUs · 8 GB each

= 80 CPUs · 320 GB

10 students in the GPU lab: 1 GPU (24 GB) each

= 10 GPUs

20 servers idle after class: stopped after an hour

= resources back to the pool

Changing the Hub Mid-Term

Week 1

values.yaml

the hub you agreed to run

Week 6

+ gpu-unit.yaml

a GPU option for the deep-learning unit

Week 9

+ dataset.yaml

this term's dataset, shared

Finals

+ finals.yaml

a longer idle timeout

After

helm uninstall

students keep their work

helm upgrade bio210 jupyterhub/jupyterhub \    -f values.yaml -f gpu-unit.yaml

Each change is a small file on top of the one you started with. Remove the file and upgrade again, and the change is gone; the base file never changes.

AI in the Classroom

35

Hosted Models in JupyterLab

  • NRP hosts open-weight models (Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, gpt-oss and more) behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint
  • Jupyter AI in JupyterLab: a chat panel, and an %%ai cell magic, pointed at NRP's models
  • Put it in your course image: students log in and use it, no token handoff
  • Or students call the models from Python, with a token from nrp.ai/llmtoken
  • Free for research and education, like the rest of NRP
Notebook cells
%load_ext jupyter_ai_magics %%ai openai-chat:qwen3Explain a p-value to a biology student in three sentences. # or from Python, with a token from nrp.ai/llmtokenfrom openai import OpenAIclient = OpenAI(base_url="https://ellm.nrp-nautilus.io/v1",                api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"])
https://nrp.ai/documentation/userdocs/ai/llm-managed/

A fallback order, not a ranking of users or models.

Every request goes to the 1st choice while it's healthy.

Only when it's down, or ejected by the health checks, does the 2nd choice answer.
